ee1fad9cbdcbdc53: KUALA LUMPUR: Deepavali may be over, but that’s no reason to stop enjoying every manner of Indian cuisine. And if you're in the mood to take things up a notch, Jwala in Bukit Damansara offers a dining experience that goes beyond the usual banana leaf meal.
Named after the Sanskrit word for fire, Jwala is an upscale Indian restaurant which has earned a place in the Michelin Guide for three consecutive years since opening in 2023.
With its sleek, contemporary interiors this restaurant makes a stylish first impression.

But the real attraction is its open kitchen, where diners watch chefs from India work their magic with a custom-built tandoor imported from the country. Fuelled by Sarawak mangrove wood charcoal, the oven is central to the signature chargrilled dishes and freshly baked breads here.
FMT Lifestyle visited Jwala for a weekday lunch and here's the verdict.
One dish that deserves a spot on every table is the Jwala Black Dal. Once you’ve tried this, and you may never look at the humble lentil dish the same way again.

Made with black lentils (urad dal), it is slow-cooked overnight using the residual heat of the tandoor's dying embers. The result is a rich, velvety preparation that has a distinct earthy, smoky flavour from the charcoal.

The perfect companion is the restaurant’s signature tandoori croissant naan, which brings together the best of two familiar favourites. Made by laminating the dough with butter, much like a French croissant, it is baked against the inner walls of the clay oven.

The result is a golden, flaky crust that crackles when torn apart, giving way to a pillowy interior with the chewiness of traditional naan. Scoop up the dal with the naan and follow it with a sip of masala chai. It is an unassuming combination, but your taste buds will beg to differ.

For something meatier, try the Angaar, a tandoor-grilled chicken dish served with fried spinach and pickled onions. The chicken is juicy and beautifully charred, with a fragrant marinade featuring toasted, cracked fennel seeds. The spices add plenty of flavour without overpowering the dish.

Those dropping by for lunch should consider the thali set, which offers a little bit of everything on one platter. It comes with tomato rasam, dal palak, jeera rice, roti, papadam, mixed pickle, papaya salad, kulfi and a cup of masala tea.
For the meat component, diners can choose either butter chicken or mutton varuval.
The butter chicken is a more refined take on the familiar favourite, with a smooth, rich gravy that allows the spices to shine without being overwhelmed by sweetness.

Although Jwala specialises in North Indian cuisine, its mutton varuval is not to be overlooked. Rather than the usual large chunks of meat, the mutton is served in strips so tender they practically fall apart with each bite.
It is also less oily than many versions, allowing the meat's natural flavour and fragrant curry leaves to shine without an overwhelming chilli kick.

Another pleasant surprise in the thali is the papaya salad. Sweet with a tangy finish, it makes for an addictive little accompaniment that is easy to keep going back to. There's plenty more to explore on the à la carte menu, from biryani and lamb chops to malai kofta.
Those seeking a more elaborate experience can opt for the seven- to nine-course tasting menus, which showcase more inventive combinations such as strawberry papdi chaat and croquettes.

Later this month, the restaurant will also collaborate with Japanese restaurant Okaju on a special tasting menu celebrating Indian and Japanese flavours. Expect creative combinations such as curry soba and caviar pani puri.
Whether you're after comforting classics or a more adventurous dining experience, Jwala serves up a compelling reason to look beyond the usual Indian fare.
Jwala E-2-01, Level 2, Block E, The Five @ KPD, 49, Jalan Dungun, Bukit Damansara, Kuala Lumpur
Business hours: 12pm–3pm; 6pm–11pm (closed on Mondays)

9bc6e6918dc53ea7: NOVEMBER 12 — Every few years, governments publish a glossy report about the future. It will be full of impressive charts, expert quotes, and bold predictions about artificial intelligence, clean energy, and the industries of tomorrow.
Then it goes on a shelf, and very little changes.

This is the strange state of “technology foresighting”. Countries know they need to do it. Technology changes constantly, and nobody wants to be the nation still building fax machines while everyone else moves to email. So governments hire experts, run workshops, and produce lots of reports.
After all that effort, are countries actually any better prepared for the future? Often, no.

The first problem is a basic misunderstanding of what foresight is for. Many people assume the goal is to predict the future: figure out exactly which technologies will matter, then invest in those. Pick the winners, avoid the losers.

The honest answer, as the European Union’s own policy lab puts it, is that foresight “will not tell you the future.” Nobody can. The value of looking ahead isn’t in making a perfect prediction. It’s in mapping out the range of possible futures, spotting the warning signs of change early, and building the flexibility to respond when surprises arrive.
When governments treat foresight as a guessing game, they end up with a list of trendy technologies to fund—and none of the agility needed when reality takes a detour, which often happens.

The second problem is that the tools themselves are showing their age. The workhorse of government foresight is something called the “Delphi method,” invented in the 1950s. The idea is simple: gather a panel of experts, ask them questions, share the answers anonymously, and repeat until everyone roughly agrees.
It’s slow. It’s expensive. And it has a well-known flaw: experts tend to converge on conventional wisdom, missing the wild cards that end up mattering most.

Interestingly, a 2026 study found that a group of large language models—AI chatbots, essentially—could stand in for human experts in these exercises and reach similar conclusions far faster and cheaper. That’s genuinely useful: it could free up human experts to focus on the harder questions of values and trade-offs, rather than the routine work of trend-spotting.
But automating the old process doesn’t fix the deeper issue. Faster reports that still gather dust are just dust gathering at higher speed.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A robot waits to serve customers at a mini market in Beijing September 22, 2026. — AFP pic

The real problem: foresight without consequence. Here’s the crux of it. The biggest obstacle isn’t methodology. It’s that foresight exercises are often disconnected from the decisions that actually matter—budgets, laws, regulations.

The United Kingdom learned this the hard way. It launched a national foresight program back in 1993, produced hundreds of recommendations, and funded plenty of them initially. But over three decades, the approach kept shifting, because one-off mega-exercises simply don’t stick. Meanwhile, Finland—a country of just 5.5 million people—built foresight directly into its political system, with a permanent parliamentary committee and a government futures report every four years. The difference isn’t smarter experts. It’s that Finland made looking ahead part of how government works, not a special project.
Think of it this way: a company that does an annual “innovation workshop” but never changes how it operates isn’t really innovating. It’s performing. Too many governments are performing foresight.
What should change?
Three things, and none of them require reinventing the wheel.

First, make foresight permanent. Instead of a big report every five years, governments need ongoing scanning—people whose actual job is to watch for weak signals and feed them into decision-making in real time. Singapore and the UK have moved in this direction. Most countries haven’t.

Second, stop pretending there’s one right method. A small country with limited resources might get more from a focused study of one critical industry than from a sprawling national exercise. Regional cooperation—like the Asean Foresight Alliance—can help smaller nations avoid duplicating effort. There’s no single template; there’s only what fits.

Third—and this is the uncomfortable one—admit that foresight is political. Every choice about which technologies to prioritize, which scenarios to explore, and whose voices count is a choice about values and power. Pretending these are purely technical matters doesn’t make them neutral. It just shuts the public out of decisions that shape their lives. Citizens have a stake in these conversations, and they should be part of them.

The countries that handle technological change best won’t be the ones with the fanciest reports or the longest list of experts. They’ll be the ones that built the habit of acting on early warnings, the courage to confront uncomfortable possibilities, and the humility to admit the future can’t be controlled—only prepared for.

9694513ae5a463a4: SINGAPORE, Nov 12 — National carrier Singapore Airlines (SIA) posted a net profit of S$134 million (RM425 million) in the first half of 2026 amid a record S$11.3 billion (RM35.8 billion) revenue, the group reported on Wednesday (November 11).

But despite total revenue growing by 16.8 per cent to better the S$9.67 billion (RM30.7 billion) revenue posted in the same period last year, net profit fell by 43.9 per cent — from S$239 million (RM758 million) in the first half of its last financial year — to S$134 million (RM425 million).
This was mainly due to high fuel costs, which grew 90.3 per cent to over S$4.7 billion (RM14.9 billion), weighing down revenue from record passenger carriage and robust cargo yield, SIA pointed out.
In the first half of its 2026/2027 financial year, SIA and Scoot saw passenger flown revenue reach nearly S$9.1 billion (RM28.8 billion) as they carried a record 21.8 million passengers.
This, as passenger yields grew 12.1 per cent to 11.1 cents per revenue passenger-kilometre, while cargo revenue grew 30.2 per cent to over S$1.39 billion (RM4.4 billion).
Meanwhile, non-fuel expenditure rose by 6.8 per cent to S$429 million (RM1.36 billion), driven by overall capacity expansion and inflationary cost increases, the group said.

Coupled with the weaker first quarter performance, and partially offset by lower share of losses from associated companies — mainly Air India — its first half net profit consequently fell by S$105 million (RM333 million) as compared to the same period last year, to S$134 million (RM425 million).

Specific to the second quarter of its current financial year, SIA’s total revenue grew by 14.3 per cent to S$5.58 billion (RM17.7 billion), while its operating profit grew by 16.3 per cent to S$463 million (RM1.47 billion).
Strong balance sheet
Despite this, SIA pointed out that it still holds one of the strongest balance sheets in the airline industry.

Its cash and bank balances grew by S$191 million (RM605 million) to S$8.12 billion (RM25.7 billion), largely due to the S$2.5 billion (RM7.9 billion) net cash from operations, and S$911 million (RM2.89 billion) in proceeds from the maturity of fixed deposits placed for tenors longer than 12 months.

These were partially offset by S$1.11 billion (RM3.5 billion) worth of capital expenditure, S$994 million (RM3.15 billion) in repayments of fixed rate bond and borrowings, and S$915 million (RM2.9 billion) in payment of ordinary and special dividends.
The group also declared that its total cash and liquidity stood at S$8.98 billion (RM28.5 billion).

This consists of the S$8.12 billion (RM25.7 billion) in cash and bank balances and S$855 million (RM2.71 billion) in fixed deposits placed for tenors longer than 12 months, classified as other short-term assets.
It also has access to S$3.23 billion (RM10.2 billion) in committed lines of credit that remain undrawn.
In the second quarter, SIA and its low-cost budget carrier Scoot, each took delivery of two new aircraft, bringing its operating fleet to 224 passenger and freighter aircraft.
The group has another 58 on order.
Outlook

And while the airline industry continues to operate in an uncertain environment, with volatile geopolitical developments adding complexity across operations and supply chains, the group said it is in a strong position to navigate these, pointing to its diversified global network and broad mix of traffic flows.
It also noted that passenger demand remains healthy, supported by seasonal travel flows, while cargo demand has been firm owing to semiconductor and cloud computing-related flows.
“The Group will maintain disciplined cost management to reinforce its long-term competitive position,” SIA added. — AsiaOne
6416dae73fb9a4c3: PETALING JAYA: Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) is unlikely to entertain attempts by pro-Barisan Nasional (BN) cybertroopers to portray the coalitions as having close political ties, an analyst says.

National Council of Professors fellow Jeniri Amir said GPS leaders were aware of attempts by certain quarters to shape public perception, particularly ahead of the state elections in Melaka and Sarawak as well as the 16th general election (GE16).

He said GPS had no need to forge an alliance with BN, at either the state or federal level, and should instead maintain its neutral position to avoid any misconceptions about its relationship with other parties.
"I believe GPS leaders are aware of what they are doing and understand the game being played by cybertroopers who are trying to give the public such an impression," he told FMT.

Last week, several pro-BN social media accounts posted pictures of deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof with Melaka chief minister Ab Rauf Yusoh, linking the meeting to GPS’s decision to contest the Sarawak election on its own without cooperating with Pakatan Harapan (PH).

However, Fadillah, who is also the energy transition and water transformation minister, clarified that his visit to Melaka was for official ministry business, to officiate the CGNEI 2026 Gas Turbine Power Generation Conference in Kuala Sungai Baru, Alor Gajah.

Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB) information chief Abdul Karim Rahman Hamzah previously reiterated that GPS would contest the Sarawak polls independently, without an electoral pact with any party from Peninsular Malaysia, although it would continue cooperating within the unity government.

Jeniri said GPS’s position as an independent local coalition capable of making its own decisions was important, particularly ahead of GE16, when the Sabah and Sarawak blocs are expected to play a significant role in determining the formation of the federal government.

He also stressed the importance of maintaining stability in the unity government until the end of its term to ensure that the government’s development agenda and Sarawak’s demands under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 could be fulfilled.
Academy of Sciences Malaysia fellow Jayum Jawan said GPS’s relationship with coalitions in Peninsular Malaysia depended largely on which side held power in Putrajaya.

He said history showed that PBB and the coalition it led were not permanently aligned with any party, pointing to the aftermath of BN’s defeat in the 2018 general election, when PBB left the coalition and formed GPS.
"PBB and the coalition it leads operate on the understanding that there are no permanent friends. What matters is who holds power, as there is no benefit in supporting a losing side," he said.
Jayum said if BN and Umno returned to power after GE16, GPS could potentially leave PH and resume cooperation with the coalition. The reverse would be true if PH remained in government, he added.

However, he said BN’s attempts to project its influence in Sarawak might not have a significant impact on voters, given that the coalition had no branches, members or grassroots machinery in the state.
Jayum said social media campaigns were more likely to reach urban voters, while most Sarawak voters lived in rural and semi-urban areas, where everyday livelihood concerns took priority.
"National issues are less effective. What matters more are bread-and-butter issues such as livelihoods, roads, water and electricity supply," he said.
677cc17ea74aef71: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters.

The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services.

On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.”

It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data.
Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud.
That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups.
Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services.

Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach.

On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility.

Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

9b79aafa4acfbd1f: WASHINGTON: In a historic upset, Democrat Scott Colom has won his US Senate race in traditionally conservative Mississippi, networks projected Wednesday, making him the first African American elected to the chamber from the southern state in more than 140 years.

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, prevailed over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in perhaps the most extraordinary seat flip of an already extraordinary US midterm election, in which Democrats crushed the Republicans to reclaim the majority in both chambers of Congress.

Colom's win in the deep South adds sting to the stunning rebuke of President Donald Trump as voters around the country shunned his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.

The latest win, called Wednesday by US news outlets that included CNN, NBC and CBS, will give Democrats 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with 44 for Republicans and one race -- in the state of Alaska -- still outstanding.

The midterms result was a personal humiliation for 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept through the Republican heartland, leaving him as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term.
The Democratic flipping of Congress signals an end to Trump's stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, probe his administration and thwart his appointments.

Including Mississippi now, Democrats flipped eight Senate seats that had been held by Republicans, scoring historic breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine -- several of which had not changed hands for decades.
Hyde-Smith, in office since 2018, conceded the race in a video posted to X.

"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," the 67-year-old senator said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

The race in ruby red Mississippi went down to the wire -- a surprise for many observers who doubted the scale of the Democratic blue wave riding on mounting anger over Trump's harsh immigration policy, the war in Iran and rising costs of living.
CNN called it for Colom on Wednesday, eight days after election night, with some 99% of the vote in and the Democrat ahead of Hyde-Smith by 49.2 %t to 48.7%, a difference of 4,585 votes.
"Blue Mississippi is here," the US Senate's top Democrat Chuck Schumer proclaimed on X after the projections came in.
"Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him."
Colom is set to become the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly 40 years, and first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era after the Civil War.
Mississippi has no law mandating a recount in the event of a tight election. But legal teams from both candidates are reported to be ramping up for potential challenges.

fc712e46e347b6e9: A child struggling to breathe should matter more than a company’s sustainability score.

That should be obvious. Yet every return of regional haze forces an uncomfortable question: are increasingly elaborate environmental, social and governance reporting requirements making the world better, or merely making corporate responsibility look better on paper?
We produce disclosures, establish committees and celebrate compliance. Meanwhile, communities need something simpler: air they can breathe without fearing what it will do to their children.

For Malaysia, the climate and haze crisis must be judged against that basic expectation. A polished sustainability report is not evidence that the people exposed to environmental harm are being protected.
The damage enters our homes
Haze is not merely an unpleasant view from an office window. Smoke contains fine particles, known as PM2.5, that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
Exposure can trigger coughing, wheezing, breathing difficulties and asthma attacks, and increase emergency visits and hospital admissions for respiratory conditions.

Children, older people, expectant mothers and those with existing heart or lung disease face greater risks. Outdoor workers face higher exposure because earning a living may require remaining outside when others can retreat indoors.
Behind these clinical descriptions are ordinary families making difficult decisions.

A parent must decide whether to take leave, arrange childcare or bring a wheezing toddler to a clinic. An older person with breathing problems faces another anxious night. A delivery rider must weigh the need for income against prolonged exposure.
The burden extends beyond treatment. Families can face transport costs, medicine bills and lost work hours. Employers must manage absences. Healthcare facilities must prepare for additional patients.
When schools close, lessons are interrupted and care arrangements become harder. Children lose opportunities to learn, play and socialise.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (Unicef) identifies lost learning and recreational opportunities among the wider consequences associated with wildfire smoke and related disruption.
The injustice is plain: protection should not depend on whether a household can afford filtered air, private treatment or time away from work.
A climate crisis with human fingerprints
Climate conditions can make fires more dangerous, but weather must not become a convenient excuse for preventable damage.

Singapore’s environment ministry has explained that healthy peatlands are wet ecosystems that do not burn spontaneously. Draining peatlands and burning vegetation create fire risks, while prolonged dry conditions can worsen the intensity of fires.
The connection runs both ways. Damaged peatlands become vulnerable to burning, while fires release stored carbon and destroy ecosystems that should help protect the climate.
Preventing haze therefore requires more than extinguishing flames. It requires responsible land management before the burning starts.
The same crisis disrupted transport, trade and tourism and forced school closures. These are historical figures, not estimates for the present episode.
Their significance is that governments and businesses have long had evidence of how destructive uncontrolled fires can become.
Make businesses answerable
ESG reporting should help expose these risks, identify responsibilities and direct resources towards prevention.
But disclosure is a means, not the destination.

A zero burning policy should prompt questions about implementation. Who monitors the land? What happens when fire risks rise? Are suppliers scrutinised? Are prevention teams adequately equipped? Can independent investigators examine what happened?

Malaysian companies with operations abroad should be expected to explain their prevention systems wherever they operate. Geographic distance cannot be a persuasive answer to questions about group oversight.
Equally, accountability requires evidence. A hotspot near a concession is a reason to investigate, not an automatic verdict of guilt.
Authorities must establish where fires occurred, who controlled the land, what duties applied, what preventive measures existed and whether failures contributed to the damage.
Sustainability reports should become documents whose claims can be tested against operational records, independent findings and actual outcomes.
Investors, too, should ask whether returns are being sustained while environmental and health costs fall on people outside the balance sheet.
Replace reassurance with consequences
Malaysia needs a public response that begins before air quality deteriorates.

Authorities should publish clear warnings, practical school and workplace protocols, and arrangements to protect vulnerable communities. Health services should prepare for increased demand, rather than leave families navigating another emergency alone.
Regional cooperation must become operational. The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution already provides for prevention, monitoring, information exchange and mutual assistance.
Governments should demonstrate how these commitments translate into timely action. What about the penalties for those nations that fail to abide by these agreements?
Regulators must turn disclosures into investigations where warranted, and findings into enforcement. Boards must take responsibility for prevention across their operations and supply chains.
Investors and lenders must demand evidence that commitments are implemented.

Where wrongdoing is proven, those responsible must face meaningful penalties and pay for the damage caused, with board members held accountable wherever the evidence and applicable law establish personal liability.
Yet what accountability, if any, have we seen at board level in Malaysia over haze linked to operations in Kalimantan?

If Malaysian companies operate there, their directors must answer legitimate questions about oversight, fire prevention and whether their sustainability commitments are being honoured beyond our borders.
The costs must not simply remain with families, healthcare workers and taxpayers.
For Malaysia and our neighbours, the demand should be unequivocal: prevent the fires, establish responsibility, enforce the law and ensure those found liable pay for the damage.
Do not ask communities choking on haze to applaud another sustainability report. Show them what changed because of it.
Fewer fires. Fewer hospital visits. Fewer school closures. Cleaner air.
That is the ESG scorecard that matters.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

d417f905ed65d8ee: A Salvadoran Army soldier stands guard at a camp in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct. 31, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty ImagesOn Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele posted footage of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince. He had earlier requested, via a social media post in Haitian Creole, the address of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal organizations. Bukele subsequently claimed the operation, conducted with Haitian police, had demolished Joseph’s residence and gang headquarters. As many as 20 people were killed, although Joseph was reportedly absent. The attack comes amid a flurry of anti-gang operations in Haiti. On Nov. 6, Mathias Saintil, head of the “Boston” gang in Cité Soleil, was killed in a drone strike by a Haitian special task force, prompting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé to declare on the social media platform X “one less gang leader.” Erik Prince, founder of the private military firm Vectus Global, responded: “Nice shot.” As an expert on organized crime in Latin America and the Caribbean, I believe these operations mark both a dramatic escalation in Haiti’s fight against organized crime and the first overseas test of Bukele’s security model. The intervention is drawing support from some regional leaders and pro-Bukele networks, even as concerns grow over civilian casualties and whether military gains can translate into lasting security. Rescue mission or military offensive? El Salvador already had a limited presence in Haiti as one of six countries contributing personnel to the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, or GSF. The force was authorized in 2025 to help Haitian authorities reclaim cities and streets from violent gangs that control swathes of the impoverished nation. But it remains severely understaffed and has struggled to translate military operations into lasting territorial gains. Then, in an Oct. 18 gang ambush, four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the Gang Suppression Force disappeared. Their burned vehicle was recovered, but their fate remains uncertain. Either way, Bukele used the incident to justify expanding El Salvador’s military presence in Haiti. Within weeks he had sent roughly 2,500 troops, along with armored vehicles and attack helicopters, in what he initially called a rescue mission. They joined an already crowded battlefield. Haiti’s police and army operate alongside the GSF, authorized but not commanded by the United Nations. The Haitian task force involved in operations against Saintil also works with former Blackwater CEO Prince’s Vectus Global, while vigilante groups patrol contested neighborhoods. Dozens of armed gangs associated with the gang coalition Viv Ansanm control large parts of Port-au-Prince and operate beyond the capital. Special forces from El Salvador ride in a Gang Suppression Force truck in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Oct 23, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images The Gang Suppression Force was authorized by the U.N. Security Council to deploy up to 5,550 personnel, and it currently has roughly 2,000 on the ground. Most of the Salvadoran troops now in Haiti operate outside its command. Haitian Prime Minister Fils-Aimé insists that Haiti directs the operations. Yet neither government has publicly disclosed the agreement specifying Salvadoran authority, rules of engagement or the deployment’s duration. Without a published deployment agreement, the chain of command and rules for authorizing strikes remain unclear to the public. Despite President Donald Trump’s support for Bukele, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has distanced Washington from the Salvadoran offensive, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He warned that poor coordination could lead to friendly fire, while U.S. diplomats formally protested the risks to multinational troops and civilian personnel. Salvadoran authorities dispute American allegations that their gunfire struck the U.S. embassy and endangered multinational troops. They also questioned the credibility of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti. Uncertain rules of engagement Haiti’s security crisis is dire. In recent years, organized violence has reached levels associated with armed conflict. Almost 6,000 people were killed in 2025, and more than 4,000 in the first nine months of 2026. Nearly 1.5 million Haitians have been displaced as of August 2026, and expanded offensives and gang reprisals could drive more from their homes. An independent legal assessment by the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights classifies fighting between Haitian forces and the Viv Ansanm coalition as a noninternational armed conflict, a legal category that includes civil wars. The International Committee of the Red Cross has separately warned of the risks to civilians, urging all sides to respect international law. The distinction matters because the rules on lethal force are different in war and policing. Both require civilians to be protected. But in an armed conflict, members of armed groups with combat roles can be targeted even when they pose no immediate threat. In a police operation, simply being suspected of gang membership is not enough to justify killing someone – lethal force is generally allowed only when necessary to protect lives. Of particular concern is the growing use of explosive drones and helicopter attacks in residential areas. At least 1,243 people were killed in 141 drone operations between March 2025 and January 2026, including at least 60 people reportedly unconnected to gangs, 17 of them children. These operations predated the Salvadoran escalation but demonstrate the risks of using explosive weapons in populated areas. At the same time, overlapping mandates for foreign troops and private military contractors could complicate investigations into civilian casualties and allegations of unlawful attacks. Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé and Col. Jose Figueroa of the Salvadoran Army address the media about security operations on Nov. 3, 2026. Clarens Siffroy/AFP via Getty Images Exporting the Bukele model Some Haitians, exhausted by insecurity, welcome the international intervention. Crowds have cheered Salvadoran soldiers, waving sticks and chanting Bukele’s name. A prominent Haitian human rights advocate supported the deployment while warning that residents of gang-controlled neighborhoods are not necessarily gang members. Bukele promotes the offensive through videos of troops and airstrikes amplified by Salvadoran officials and pro-government influencers. Messages in Haitian Creole and Spanish that portray the strikes as victories against gangs closely resemble the government’s widely circulated footage of mass arrests and prison transfers in El Salvador. Under Bukele, who came to power in 2019, homicides in El Salvador have plummeted, boosting a belief in parts of South America and the Caribbean that an iron fist approach to gang violence is worth the associated cost to human rights. Indeed, security hardliners across Latin America have pointed to El Salvador’s falling homicide rate to justify similar crackdowns. Dominican President Luis Abinader has endorsed the intervention and confirmed logistical and intelligence cooperation. Yet the Salvadoran model has relied on emergency powers and mass incarceration. Around 1.7% of Salvadorans are imprisoned – by far the highest rate in the world. Haiti presents greater operational challenges. According to the U.N. Office for Drugs and Crime, gangs hold extensive territory, possess heavy weapons and maintain connections to political and commercial networks. Haitian institutions are weaker, and children are widely recruited into armed groups from a young age. Sustaining territorial gains would require functioning police and courts, along with protection for residents after foreign troops leave. The expanded Salvadoran presence in Haiti also carries political risks for both governments. Bukele is seeking a third term in February 2027, following constitutional changes that removed presidential term limits. Salvadoran military casualties could stir criticism at home and pressure him to escalate, particularly with the four Salvadoran technicians whose disappearance prompted the rescue mission still missing. For his part in Haiti, Fils-Aimé has publicly backed the offensive ahead of Haiti’s elections, scheduled for July and October 2027. Civilian casualties or failure to sustain gains could undermine his own government’s credibility. Beyond military operations The deployment may foreshadow wider regional security arrangements. El Salvador belongs to the U.S.-backed Shield of the Americas, a coalition launched by Trump in March 2026 to expand military cooperation against drug cartels and other transnational criminal groups. The Salvadoran operation in Haiti does not formally fall under that initiative, whose 15 signatories have pledged closer security cooperation. But such partnerships could allow regional governments to deploy forces with American logistical support while limiting direct U.S. military involvement. Although the Salvadoran operation is the latest high-profile example, I have seen similar cycles working in Haiti since the 2000s. U.N. peacekeepers and Haitian police cleared parts of Cité Soleil between 2007 and 2009, contributing to a decline in kidnappings but failing to deliver lasting security. The U.N. mission later introduced cholera following the 2010 earthquake, killing more than 9,000 people and prompting an eventual apology from the U.N. Gangs endure because their economic networks survive military offensives. They profit from kidnappings and illicit trade while controlling access to key roads and markets. Removing leaders can weaken organizations without ending these revenue streams. While the current Salvadoran offensive may deliver short-term security gains, sustaining them will depend on Haitian institutions maintaining control of recovered territory. Bukele’s intervention is now an overseas test of a security model with considerable political appeal. But its consequences will ultimately be measured by whether Haitians are safer when foreign forces depart. Robert Muggah is the co-founder of the Igarapé Institute, and a principal of the SecDev Group. He also advises governments, private companies, non-profits and international organizations such as the United Nations, the IMF and the World Bank.

d5227a85f3e0f37b: I’m not an expert on highways or infrastructure, but I drive a lot because of necessity, and also because I like being on the road. I’ve done at least 1.5 million kilometres in my life, and I have a bad back and knees and rather diminished retirement savings because of it.

Malaysia has an amazing network of highways and federal and state roads. They’re the literal backbone of our national development, and having put in around 200,000km of driving abroad, I can say that our roads aren’t too bad at all.

There’s a caveat though. For the money we’ve spent on them, they should’ve been much better. I’d give an A minus for the overall national road architecture, though only a C for that in Kuala Lumpur, and another C for the design, construction and maintenance of these roads, especially the newer ones. And it’s an E and very close to an F for the lack of transparency about their ownership, costs and toll charges.

The financial incentives of owning a highway concession, as well as the benefits of political patronage (read: corruption) in parcelling out these concessions to favoured parties leaves quite a sour taste. Our great highways and networks come at too high a cost borne by taxpayers, and especially highway users. It need not have been this way.

My biggest concern is that Malaysia is turning into a car society the same way as the US. Cars seem to be the answer to everything. We’re building out our cities, towns, suburbia, villages, industrial parks, public highways and private turnpikes as if motor vehicles are the only means of transport.

Kuala Lumpur’s downtown area is reasonably compact, but try walking from one point to another. The route would either be inconvenient, dangerous or downright impossible. Everywhere we go, cars get priority and pedestrians and non-motorised cyclists are left to fend for themselves.

We’ve convinced ourselves that our climate is too hot, humid and rainy, and that our roads are too dangerous and inconvenient. There is certainly some truth there, but mostly because the original designs of our living spaces didn’t provide much in the way of alternatives to motorised vehicles.
Addicted to cars

Unfortunately, the manufacture, import and ownership of cars and the taxes and duties due on them makes them too critical to our economy, one of the largest car markets in the region. Cars are a drug we’re unable or unwilling to give up because of the negative impact on our economic health. So, we take higher and higher doses of this “drug” and convince ourselves it is vital to our existence and prosperity.

But the world is changing. Car ownership, especially in mature economies, is not growing by leaps and bounds any more. Certainly, electric vehicles (EVs) are addressing some of the problems associated with them such as pollution, use of environmentally destructive fossil fuels etc. But even if we end up with EVs replacing all fossil fuel vehicles, we still wouldn't have made much progress.

Part of our love affair is certainly psychological. Many Malaysians, myself included, are first-time car owners. Car ownership is an important milestone in our life, often a sign that we’ve reached a certain level of success in life. We haven’t become inured to cars the way many in the more developed societies have. You can take our cars away, as the saying goes, only from our cold dead hands.

But our children and grandchildren aren’t heading that way. Populations are increasingly being concentrated in massive urban conurbations, with such population growth, often caused by urban migration, leading to huge megalopolises such as Jakarta, Mexico City, Lagos etc as well as to the older ones such as Tokyo and Los Angeles.

The coming generations will not have the same love affair with cars as we do. Cars will be just a means of getting from A to B and no longer an important milestone in their life. Many cities are increasingly building out alternative urban transport systems such as light rail, monorail and trams, as well as simpler solutions such as climate-controlled walkways and corridors to cater to the needs of their growing but less car-fixated population.
What lies ahead

Technology recognises this change. The latest self-driving EVs aren’t meant to help us drive our cars better, but rather to create a market where we can just dial up a driverless car that can take us to wherever we need to go without having to own such cars or deal with their drivers.
It will create a new business of the car-as-a-service, with cars used on subscription or rented from manufacturers the same way as computer software has been for quite a while.

We risk leaving behind a vast network of expensive but underutilised roads as well as unfit, unhealthy people whose lives are overly spent in the air-conditioned comforts of their houses, cars, offices or shopping malls.

The focus on cars also means rail is often neglected. We’re just beginning to start operating the East Coast Railway Link (ECRL), and even then both its reason for existence and its long-term sustainability are in doubt. Rail can’t win against cars because of the huge capital costs and timeframes involved, unless the government is willing to tip the scales in its favour through incentives and disincentives to the rakyat.

We have over 5,000km of expressways, over half of which are tolled, and the rest would likely end up being tolled too. The appetite to build more highways, driven by politics and surging demand caused by escalating car ownership, will just mean that more toll highways with E designations and fancy names will appear.

It’s not all or nothing. We can both benefit from the economics of car ownership and prepare for a future where cars are not that critical to our lives any more. We need the political will to make alternatives to just having more and more cars and more and more roads for them to drive on.
Read also: A journey through a tangled web of highways and byways

fa483c45db8466fb: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Scientists have discovered a bizarre “invisible” object in space that challenges our understanding of stellar evolution and could help resolve longstanding astronomical mysteries, according to a study published on Wednesday in Science Advances. Its orbit and mass are so strange, in fact, that researchers ran thousands of simulations and couldn’t reproduce them.

The hidden object is likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star, which is the collapsed core that is left over after a massive star goes supernova. Located in a system called J0008+0128,, the object was detected through its gravitational effects on its companion, a red giant star.

Massive stars that go supernova either collapse into neutron stars or black holes, both of which belong to a wider family of dead stars known as “stellar remnants.” But for decades, astronomers have puzzled over the so-called “mass gap" between neutron stars and black holes, which is the observed scarcity of remnants between 2.5 and five times as massive as the Sun.

The object lurking in J0008+0128 could be up to 2.8 times as massive as the Sun, which “potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes,” according to the new study. The colossal mass, combined with its unusually wide orbit of 1,218 days, challenge our understanding of how these objects form.

“We search for compact objects (mainly neutron stars and black holes) using large spectroscopic surveys,” said Song Wang, an associate researcher at the National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences, who co-authored the study, in an email to 404 Media. “We have found more than 10 neutron stars, and J0008+0128 is the most massive one among them.”

Generally speaking, stars that are over 25 times as massive as the Sun will form black holes, while stars that are about 10-to-25 times as massive will become neutron stars. Stars with masses similar to the Sun, meanwhile, are destined to spend their afterlives as white dwarfs, which are much larger and less dense than neutron stars. For instance, neutron stars are mere miles in diameter, whereas white dwarfs are about the size of Earth.

Because they are dense pressure cookers, neutron stars are filled with disassembled components of atoms, especially neutrons—hence the name—but also protons and electrons. Supermassive neutron stars like the one in J0008+0128 can shed light on the poorly understood “equation of state” in these objects, which is the relationship between their immense pressures and densities.

“The equation of state of neutron stars is a long-standing unsolved problem in astrophysics, and neutron star masses can provide crucial observational tests,” said Wang. “This is particularly true for massive neutron stars: how massive a neutron star can become depends on how ‘stiff’ its internal matter is in resisting gravitational collapse.”

“The discovery and measurement of supermassive neutron stars (i.e., those above two solar masses) can place important constraints on the equation of state of matter at extreme densities, helping to identify the theories that truly describe the behavior of matter under such extreme conditions,” he added.

In other words, J0008+0128 could open a window into the churning atomic stew within these exotic objects. But the system is weird for reasons beyond the supermassive object lurking in the dark. Indeed, the team ran thousands of simulations but none of them “reproduced physical and orbital properties similar to J0008+0128,” according to the study.

The wide orbit between the neutron star and the red giant star is particularly difficult to explain. Neutron stars could become supermassive by gravitationally tugging material off of their stellar companions, but this object is too far away from the red giant for this mechanism to make sense.

“In fact, many compact objects discovered in recent years cannot be explained by standard binary evolution models and supernova mechanisms,” Wang noted, citing two other examples, known as Gaia BH2 and G3425.

Wang and his colleagues proposed a few alternate scenarios to account for these outliers. It may simply be that supernovas can form supermassive neutron stars within the mass gap in rare cases. The researchers also speculated that this system once contained three objects, and that two of them merged together to form the supermassive neutron star.

“There may be two massive stars forming an inner binary,” Wang explained. “They can merge at different stages. For example, a neutron star merges with a normal star, or two neutron stars merge. Either case could produce the supermassive neutron star that we observe today.”
“In addition, if J0008+0128 formed through single-star evolution, its discovery would suggest that supernovae can produce massive neutron stars,” he added.

Studying systems like J0008+0128 could illuminate the murky limits that determine the afterlives of massive stars. They are also helpful for understanding the dynamics of neutron star mergers, which scientists can detect through gravitational waves, which are ripples in spacetime.

Wang and his colleagues were able to make this new discovery with the help of sophisticated sky surveys, including astrometric data from Europe’s Gaia space telescope. The team hopes that the forthcoming data release from Gaia, due out next month, will help to narrow down the possible mass of the unseen object in J0008+0128.

“The discovery of J0008+0128, together with other systems discovered in these years (e.g., Gaia BH2 and G3425), suggests that much work remains to be done on binary evolution and supernova explosion theory,” Wang concluded.

36fe20458ab3346e: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.
The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

34b737938b531fa1: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources.

Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed.
Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing.
Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade.

Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period.
Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase.

Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster, as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030.

This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters.

Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies.
For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue.
"Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam.
"As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need."

Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

350f41e59919203e: The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party. Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy? The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering. Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.” Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change. Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip. During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles. Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act. On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change. World leaders arrive at Cop31, but what will be the role of the unofficial US delegation? Data centres are big issue The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all. Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions. After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”. Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy. However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be. The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023. Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives. They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this. What does this mean globally? What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at Cop with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies. Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution. While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power. 5fbec81ac7cecc8c: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong.
This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data.

The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica.

Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape.

Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error.
To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today.
In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said.

He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image.

"Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said.

Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

2ef828b51c4bc407: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

5f8e26b36ac467ac: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time.
Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go.
The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal.

Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration.

The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for.
Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places.

That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory.
Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds.
For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit, but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro.

The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal.
Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones.
The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®
