7f152ca6be50c785: From Moaz Nair

For generations, higher education functioned as a cornerstone of the Malaysian social contract. A tertiary degree, achieved through rigorous academic adherence, effectively guaranteed upward socioeconomic mobility and entry into the professional middle class.
Today, however, structural shifts induced by advanced automation and artificial intelligence have fundamentally fractured this predictable linear trajectory.

While aggregate macroeconomic indicators present a resilient domestic economy, micro-level data from the labour market reveals a systemic disruption. The proliferation of generative AI tools has effectively dismantled the entry-level tier of corporate employment, placing the return on investment of a traditional university degree under severe scrutiny.
Are educators in our higher educational institutions prepared to embrace this technology?

Data from the statistics department illustrates the depth of this structural paradox. While the national unemployment rate stands at a remarkably healthy 2.9%, youth unemployment (ages 15 to 24) remains stubbornly elevated at 10.1%, representing approximately 291,300 young citizens experiencing market-entry barriers.
Of more concern is the pervasive rise of skills-related underemployment.

According to the latest graduate statistics, 32.2% of the employed graduate workforce, or 1.6 million people occupy roles categorised as semi-skilled or low-skilled. The visual narrative of tertiary-educated youth operating within the gig economy or basic service sectors rather than corporate offices is no longer an anomaly; it is an empirical trend.
Young people who would normally have gone into routine professional jobs are now serving customers in tea shops. This is not what our youth aspire to.

Historically, entry-level positions served a dual purpose: they fulfilled corporate administrative needs while acting as a vital practical apprenticeship for fresh graduates. Tasks such as data compilation, minute-taking, draft formulation, and presentation synthesis allowed new entrants to internalise corporate culture, systemic hierarchies, and operational soft skills.

With AI software now executing these routine, algorithmic tasks at a fraction of the temporal and financial cost, private firms are actively reducing their junior headcounts and altering hiring thresholds.

Emerging market analysis suggests that up to 40% of standard roles historically allocated to fresh graduates have undergone severe contractions due to routine automation. Consequently, universities face an immediate existential mandate.
Institutions can no longer function as passive, credential-issuing entities, or they risk producing graduates equipped only with obsolete paper qualifications.

To prevent a structural underemployment crisis from solidifying into permanent socioeconomic inequality, a comprehensive paradigm shift must occur across institutional curricula. The traditional instructional methodology predicated on stagnant, rote-learning lectures and memory-based assessments is fundamentally incompatible with an economy wherein raw information retrieval is instant and costless.

Higher education institutions must intentionally pivot towards developing capabilities that lie beyond the current frontier of machine learning. This requires an academic focus on high-order cognitive processes, including multi-system thinking, advanced cross-disciplinary innovation, ethical governance, and sophisticated emotional intelligence.

Recognising the urgency of this transition, the higher education ministry has proactively initiated key systemic changes, recently undertaking a comprehensive review of 455 public university study programmes.

The ministry has set an aggressive target to integrate foundational AI components into 80% of all public undergraduate courses, alongside the ongoing expansion of specialised entities like the Faculty of Artificial Intelligence at Universiti Teknologi Malaysia.
The broader national blueprint aims to generate 30,000 highly skilled AI graduates by 2030 to mitigate the effects of rapid workspace automation.

However, transforming formal degree structures is merely one component of a holistic strategy. A real-world equilibrium requires immediate, coordinated fiscal and policy interventions executed in tandem with industry demands. To successfully navigate this transition, public and private stakeholders must scale up initiatives across three essential pillars.

First, academic faculties must build institutionalised, dynamic bridges with corporate partners. This collaboration ensures that university modules adjust symmetrically alongside rapidly evolving technological frontiers, shifting student assessment metrics toward practical problem-solving.

Second, leveraging national frameworks like the New Industrial Master Plan 2030 and substantial public sector technology allocations, universities must aggressively channel funds into high-performance computing infrastructure, advanced hardware acquisition, and research commercialisation funds.

Finally, stakeholders must expand lifelong reskilling ecosystems. This means scaling up structural upskilling pipelines such as micro-credentials and technical courses certified by agencies like TalentCorp or funded through HRD Corp to swiftly transition underemployed or displaced workers into high-growth, non-routine fields like semiconductor IC design, cybersecurity, and digital health.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence software does not inherently dictate the obsolescence of the university system; rather, it demands its radical re-engineering. If higher education institutions fail to adapt, the domestic economy risks widening its structural inequalities, trapping a large segment of the domestic talent pool in low-value service roles while a thin, technologically elite class captures the premium of digital growth.

Higher education must act with proactive foresight and structural courage. By transforming the curriculum from a static knowledge repository into a dynamic incubator for uniquely human innovation, Malaysian universities can ensure that their graduates remain the primary architects of the national digital economy.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

a389df548db6df1c: This has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars—from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today—a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order.
Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.
On the political front, Chinese president Xi Jinping has ruthlessly eliminated all potential opposition and centralised power in his own hands.

His decimation of the state, party, provincial, and military leadership has left a trail of bodies and resentment, even if the impenetrability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) makes this difficult to establish definitively.
With blood and revenge hammering in their heads (to paraphrase Shakespeare), numerous humiliated and disgruntled former officials could make Xi’s succession, whenever it comes, disorderly.

Cycles of apparent calm leading to chaos are not uncommon in Chinese history. They are intrinsic to what Francis Fukuyama has called the country’s “Bad Emperor” problem, with Mao Zedong and Xi representing the bad emperors of the Communist era.

On the economic front, the outlook is mixed, but downside risks are growing. Where some see an all-conquering powerhouse marrying technology to mass manufacturing, others see an economy dragged into a structural slowdown by population ageing, a prolonged property market slump, rising youth unemployment, and growing hostility to private enterprise.

Making matters worse, the long-standing source of Chinese dynamism—exports—is vulnerable to policy responses from the US and Europe, which are under immense pressure to address the latest China shock.

But perhaps even more worrying is China’s fraying fiscal capacity. Warnings about unsustainable public debt are growing louder everywhere, but the situation in China is distinctive, owing to how it manages—or, rather, fails to manage—taxation.

Few states are as successful as China when it comes to surveilling and controlling the population. But taxes represent a reciprocal bargain with citizens, who accept expropriation as legitimate on the understanding that they will get something in return: stability, public goods, improved standards of living, redistribution, and so forth. That is why wars and even empires can be lost when a state loses its capacity to tax its citizens.
The fate of the Ming and Qing dynasties is telling in this respect. Even discounting for the obvious historical differences, these episodes have faint echoes in developments today.

We recently mapped China’s taxes and revenues since 1952. Two features stand out. First, and somewhat surprisingly, the CPC has not presided over a particularly strong fiscal state. Instead, it has raised a substantial share of resources without explicitly taxing its people.

Until the late 1970s, about half the resources raised came from profits of state-owned enterprises; and in the last two decades, about one-sixth (and as much as one-quarter at its peak in 2020) has come from land sales.
In other words, China has never managed to raise sufficient sums of money via personal income taxation, even during a period of extraordinary economic vibrancy.

Over the last decade, its tax revenues from the personal income tax averaged just 1.2% of GDP. Ironically, a communist state ideologically committed to collective ownership of the means of production has had to raise revenue by divesting itself of that most sacred input, land. Evidently, the CPC can make the Chinese cower in silence, but finds it difficult to reach into their pocketbooks.
The second and even more relevant finding is that, regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for about a decade.

For example, taxes (excluding social-insurance contributions) collapsed by nearly six percentage points between 2012 and 2025, from 18.4% of GDP to 12.6%. These are levels associated with a struggling, lower-middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower.
It is difficult to say how much of this decline is attributable to growth falling below what headline figures indicate, and how much to weakening enforcement capacity.

Either way, it seems that the government grew so reliant on nontax revenues that it found itself with no options when they dried up. Whether it can change course and impose taxes on the population very much remains to be seen.
The Chinese state could find itself triply exposed—to a succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally.

In short, China’s entire growth and fiscal model, along with the social contract between the state and its citizens—coveted stability and material prosperity for restricted freedom and muzzled voice—may be in trouble.
Of course, any warning about China’s potential descent into disorder must contend with the CPC’s remarkable record of coercive control.

A slow bleed of anemic growth, rising restiveness, and deteriorating services is perhaps likelier. But even if the Chinese miracle ends with a whimper rather than a bang, the consequences may well be yet another global shock.
Navneeraj Sharma is an energy economist. Arvind Subramanian is a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

bb81a080181292fa: Di Malaysia hari ini ada suatu dilema yang mempunyai implikasi besar terhadap bagaimana Islam perlu dipelajari dan didakwahkan. Ia merangkumi isu derma untuk membayar saman fitnah seorang ahli politik dari parti yang dilaungkan sebagai pejuang Islam, dan derma untuk melunaskan denda hukuman rasuah seorang pemimpin parti politik yang melaungkan kaum Melayu sebagai perjuangan utama.

Dari pemerhatian saya, kalau kes fitnah dan rasuah itu bersifat circumstantial atau agak pudar dan banyak lubang pembuktian, saya tidak akan menulis artikel ini kerana derma bagi kedua-duanya boleh saja dihalalkan dari kaca mata perjuangan Islam atau nasional, tetapi dari apa yang saya faham tentang bukti dan pembicaraan kes-kes, semuanya sahih dan terbaik maka tidak ada keraguan dalam proses pengadilan. Namun demikian, derma untuk membayar saman fitnah dan derma untuk bantu bayar denda hukuman rasuah telah dilancarkan. Yang peliknya penjawat rasmi agama, pendakwah terkenal agama dan profesor agama sepi terhadap sama ada praktis sedemikian layak dikaitkan dengan nilai Islam. Maka itu, terpaksalah saya menulis sesuatu sebagai semacam peringatan.

Sebagai seorang yang telah membina kesedaran Islam di Amerika Syarikat sewaktu belajar jurusan seni bina di bawah tajaan JPA, saya telah menambah banyak ilmu tentang Islam melalui pembacaan koleksi hadis seperti daripada Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Muwatta, Tirmidhi, An-Nasai dan Ibn Madjah, serta menelaah tafsiran al-Quran oleh Muhammad Assad, Abdullah Yusof Ali, Hamka dan Abul A'la Maududi. Penelitian peribadi ini membawa saya kepada banyak buku tentang kerohanian, politik dan aspek sosial Islam. Dalam banyak bacaan saya, ayat dari surah al-Baqarah ini menjadi pedoman kepada saya tentang 'politik Islam';

"Bukanlah perkara kebajikan itu hanya kamu menghadapkan muka ke pihak timur dan barat, tetapi kebajikan itu ialah berimannya seseorang kepada Allah, dan hari akhirat, dan segala malaikat, dan segala kitab, dan sekalian nabi; dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya, -- kepada kaum kerabat, dan anak-anak yatim dan orang-orang miskin dan orang yang terlantar dalam perjalanan, dan kepada orang-orang yang meminta, dan untuk memerdekakan hamba-hamba abdi; dan mengerjanya seseorang akan sembahyang serta mengeluarkan zakat; dan perbuatan orang-orang yang menyempurnakan janjinya apabila mereka membuat perjanjian; dan ketabahan orang-orang yang sabar dalam masa kesempitan, dan dalam masa kesakitan, dan juga dalam masa bertempur dalam perjuangan perang Sabil. (Orang yang demikian sifatnya), mereka itulah orang yang benar (beriman dan mengerjakan kebajikan); dan mereka itulah juga orang yang bertaqwa. (al-Baqarah ayat 177)

Dari ayat ini saya boleh membina masyarakat yang baik, saya boleh membina hubungan kerohanian dengan tuhan dan saya juga boleh merancang sebuah perbandaran serta seni binanya untuk manusia. Ayat ini cukup meyakinkan saya kepada apa sebenarnya politik Islam iaitu memimpin manusia ke arah kemanusiaan sejati.

"Bukanlah perkara kebajikan itu hanya kamu menghadapkan muka ke pihak timur dan barat, tetapi kebajikan itu ialah berimannya seseorang kepada Allah, dan hari akhirat, dan segala malaikat, dan segala kitab, dan sekalian nabi; dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya" memberi definisi 'kebaikan' atau righteousness iaitu bukan sekadar ibadah ritual tetapi merangkumi suatu kesejagatan kemanusiaan di mana orang Islam perlu berkawan dengan semua manusia yang mempercayai konsep ketuhanan, penghakiman akhir, kewujudan malaikat dan pendidikan melalui kitab-kitab lama berkait dengan rasul-rasul yang kita semua umat Islam kena hafal nama dan kewujudan mereka. Kita pun tahu bahawa sejarah rasul-rasul berkait rapat dengan sejarah dan kepercayaan agama Yahudi dan Kristian. Saya memahami bahagian pertama ini sebagai suatu ajakan untuk umat Islam bersaudara dengan penganut dua agama tersebut. Namun demikian kita kini berseteru dengan kedua-duanya dari sudut politik kenegaraan.

"...dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya, -- kepada kaum kerabat, dan anak-anak yatim dan orang miskin dan orang yang terlantar dalam perjalanan, dan kepada orang yang meminta, dan untuk memerdekakan hamba-hamba abdi" bagi saya adalah tentang suatu sistem sosial yang bukan sahaja untuk sesebuah negara yang mengamalkan hukum dan nilai Islam tetapi juga tanggungjawab setiap muslim untuk membantu golongan yang berkeperluan seperti anak yatim piatu, musafir, yang meminta dan yang memerlukan bantuan kerana keperitan hidup. Kadang-kadang saya hairan apabila dalam sesebuah bandar yang dipimpin orang Islam ada ribu rakyat homeless berbagai kaum tetapi kita punyai rumah ibadat seperti masjid, gereja, kuil dan sebagainya dalam jumlah beratus buah. Sebagai umat kita lebih suka melihat bangunan ibadat beratus juta kecantikannya tetapi membiarkan yang berkeperluan merana sendiri. Siapa agaknya kena jawab di akhirat nanti.

"...dan mengerjanya seseorang akan sembahyang serta mengeluarkan zakat; dan perbuatan orang yang menyempurnakan janjinya apabila mereka membuat perjanjian; dan ketabahan orang yang sabar dalam masa kesempitan, dan dalam masa kesakitan, dan juga dalam masa bertempur dalam perjuangan perang Sabil. (Orang yang demikian sifatnya), mereka itulah orang yang benar (beriman dan mengerjakan kebajikan); dan mereka itulah juga orang yang bertakwa" saya fahami sebagai hubungan peribadi kita dengan Tuhan dalam ibadat khusus seperti bersembahyang, dan merenggangkan kita dengan harta benda sebelum kita menemui-Nya. Umat Islam juga diseru untuk menjadi profesional dalam muamalah perjanjian dan tanggungjawab antara manusia tidak kira dari kaum mana atau agama apa, saya kira.

Dalam surah al-Baqarah ayat 177 jelas tiada berkeperluan kita umat Islam untuk merenggangkan kita dengan harta dan wang demi membantu derma bagi membayar saman fitnah yang jelas terbukti tanpa was-was serta juga menderma kepada pembayaran denda hukuman rasuah yang juga terjelas tanpa was-was proses keadilannya.
Jadi, untuk kita orang Melayu dan Islam kat mana atau 'tang' mana kita nak selit amalan kita untuk menjayakan hidup sebagai Muslim yang sejati dan ikhlas membuat kebaikan?

Kalau parti-parti yang menghadapi musibah lalu ahli dan pemimpinnya menggunakan wang tabung parti sendiri tanpa derma maka boleh juga diterima alasan 'strategi politik' agar tidak hilang kerusi dan tidak merendahkan maruah ahli serta parti, walaupun konsep nilai Islam masih lagi boleh dipersoalkan. Tetapi melancarkan derma dan mengajak 'kebajikan' daripada umat Islam untuk 'membantu' musibah yang al-Quran tidak pernah sebut, itu suatu perkara yang cukup problematic dalam usaha menguar-uarkan Islam sebagai agama kemanusiaan terbaik. Walaupun Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan ada buat fatwa bahawa membantu orang yang didapati bersalah oleh mahkamah hukumnya harus, tetapi ia bersyarat iaitu si pesalah perlu mengaku kesalahan dan bertaubat tidak akan membuatnya lagi. Saya tak dengar pun Dr Siti Mastura Muhammad atau Najib Razak berbuat demikian.
Kalau dulu ada buku 'Dilema Melayu', saya kira tiba masanya ada buku 'Dilema Muslim' untuk sama-sama kita renungkan pengakhiran kita dan negara.

b5623db3fc4b9902: From Zander Lim

Recent criminal breach of trust (CBT) prosecutions involving corporate directors, senior executives and individuals entrusted with institutional funds have renewed attention to the distinction between corporate mismanagement and criminal liability.
Among these are recent prosecutions involving former executives of UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd and companies associated with Lembaga Tabung Haji.
These cases raise an important legal question: Does an unauthorised financial transaction, breach of corporate procedures or failure of governance necessarily constitute CBT?

In 2026, several CBT prosecutions were reported, including those involving a former senior military officer in relation to RM3 million belonging to the Armed Forces welfare fund; two company directors involving RM10.55 million connected with a glove manufacturing venture; former executives of three companies concerning contractor penalty payments; and the former CEO of UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd involving approximately RM37.37 million allocated for a solar photovoltaic project.
The accused persons have pleaded not guilty, and the allegations remain subject to judicial determination.

Although these prosecutions involve different transactions and circumstances, they raise important legal questions concerning entrustment, corporate authority and the element of dishonesty required to establish criminal breach of trust.
What is criminal breach of trust?
In simple terms, CBT occurs when a person entrusted with someone else's money or property dishonestly misuses it.
Under Section 405 of the Penal Code, the prosecution must generally prove three matters:
(a) Entrustment: the accused was given responsibility for, or control over, the money or property.
(b) Misuse: the accused used or dealt with it in a manner prohibited by law.
(c) Dishonesty: the accused acted dishonestly, rather than merely making a mistake or exercising poor judgment.
Section 409 provides heavier punishment where CBT is committed by certain persons, including public servants and agents.
Importantly, not every unauthorised payment or breach of company procedures amounts to CBT. Dishonesty must still be established.
When does mismanagement become a criminal offence?
Companies may suffer financial losses arising from poor investment decisions, inadequate due diligence, improper approvals or failures in corporate governance.
However, a bad business decision is not necessarily a criminal offence.

For example, Illustration (d) to Section 405 recognises that a person who acts contrary to instructions but genuinely believes the decision would benefit the owner of the property may not have committed CBT, although civil liability may arise.
Conversely, Section 409A makes clear that recording a transaction in the company's accounts does not automatically protect a person from criminal liability.
In other words, a transaction is not necessarily criminal merely because company procedures were breached, nor is it necessarily lawful simply because it was properly recorded or approved.
What matters is whether the money or property was dishonestly misused in circumstances falling within Section 405.
Corporate seniority
In corporate organisations, financial decisions often involve several levels of management, including directors, finance departments and authorised signatories.

Holding a senior position does not necessarily mean that an individual controlled every company transaction. Similarly, approving a payment does not automatically establish dishonest misappropriation.

In determining whether CBT has been committed, consideration must be given to the accused's control over the funds, the purpose of the transaction, the scope of authority and whether the evidence establishes dishonest intention.

In cases involving abetment under Sections 107 and 109 of the Penal Code, criminal liability cannot be established merely because an individual occupied a supervisory position or participated in an approval process.
The prosecution must establish the relevant acts and legal requirements constituting abetment.
Criminal liability must be based on the individual's actual conduct, not merely the position he or she held.
The recent CBT prosecutions highlight the importance of proper financial controls, clear approval procedures and accountability in corporate management.
Nevertheless, financial irregularities, breaches of internal policies and unsuccessful business decisions do not automatically amount to criminal wrongdoing.
Ultimately, the distinction between corporate mismanagement and CBT is not determined by the amount of money involved, the seniority of the accused or whether company procedures were breached.
It depends on whether the accused dishonestly misused money or property entrusted to him or her in a manner prohibited by law.
This distinction is essential to ensuring that genuine criminal misconduct is addressed without treating every failure of corporate governance as a criminal offence.
Zander Lim is an advocate solicitor and managing partner of Law Chambers of Zander Lim.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

c6db132144c32013: Diego Radames/GettyThis week, around 80 world leaders – including Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – will descend on the coastal Turkish city of Antalya for the annual United Nations climate summit, COP31. For the first time, the summit duties will be shared; Turkey will play host, while Australia leads negotiations. At home, these national leaders have no shortage of issues to contend with: the challenges of AI, major wars and declining trust in democracy. Yet looming over all of them is the existential threat posed by a heating planet. Climate change is a truly global challenge. Greenhouse gases have no respect for national boundaries, and the devastating impacts are being felt everywhere. We don’t have a world government, but we do have processes of international diplomacy to hammer out shared commitments. This is how the world is trying to deal with the climate crisis. It can be easy to be pessimistic, but COP31 can still deliver real progress. In Antalya, countries will consider a global electrification target to hasten the shift from coal, oil and gas toward clean electricity. If agreement can be found, this will be a major step forward. Remind me, what is a COP? When scientific consensus emerged on global warming in the 1980s, countries negotiated and signed a new framework on climate change in Rio De Janeiro in 1992. Since then, diplomats and negotiators have met annually for the UN’s Conference of Parties (COP) to discuss how to address dangerous human-made climate change. These talks have become huge, attended by tens of thousands of delegates every year. This year, the 31st COP is being held in Antalya, Turkey. After three decades of climate talks, countries are turning the tide on emissions. Many are transitioning away from fossil fuels, if not at the speed required. Overall, global emissions held roughly flat in 2025, though lower wildfire and land-use emissions masked continued growth from fossil fuels. Yes, the annual UN climate talks are beset by challenges. The United States has withdrawn completely. Countries are not on track to limit warming to agreed levels. Governments can’t even agree when to release the next report on global warming to guide negotiations. In some ways it’s a miracle these talks achieve anything. Agreements must be reached by consensus and endorsed by 190-plus countries, from petro-states in the Middle East to vulnerable island nations in the Pacific. Consensus is both strength and weakness. When agreements are reached, they have great legitimacy. The 2015 Paris Agreement came after two decades of hard-fought negotiations. The agreement was a monumental achievement. But consensus also means COP decisions tend to be “lowest-common-denominator” outcomes, representing incremental progress. Again and again, politics and diplomacy fall short of what the science says is required. Still, if we take a long view, we can see the UN climate talks have helped avoid the most catastrophic global warming and are transforming economies. A demonstrator holds a banner showing the 1.5°C mark, as demonstrators march past the Reichstag building in Berlin, Germany, in April to protest for renewable energies. The UN has confirmed the world will overshoot 1.5°C in the next few years. Photo by Omer Messinger/Getty Images How the Paris Agreement is working At the heart of the Paris Agreement is the goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C above the long-term average. This requires the global economy to get to net-zero emissions by the middle of this century. To get there, countries agreed to set emissions targets and increase these every five years. While these targets are slowly cutting emissions and limiting warming they are still clearly insufficient. Before the Paris Agreement, the world was on track for a cataclysmic 4°C degrees of warming this century. The first wave of emissions targets brought this below 3°C. The 2025 round of targets suggests countries may limit warming to 2.6°C. Every fraction of a degree matters. With more ambitious policies, we could theoretically still peak warming at 1.8C and return below 1.5°C later this century through investment in carbon dioxide removal. However, this would take a radical step-change in ambition. Since Paris, more than 130 countries have set long-term targets to achieve net-zero emissions. Countries have begun to signal the end of the fossil fuel era. At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, countries agreed to “phase down coal”. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023 they agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”. The task now is to make good on these promises. Taken together, COP commitments act as a market signal. This year, global investment in clean energy hit A$3.2 trillion – twice as much as investment in coal, oil and gas. Renewables also overtook coal as the world’s biggest source of electricity. A new age of electricity For COP31, there is a push for an electrification target of “35 by 35”. Both Turkey and Australia are pressing for a global commitment to increase the share of the energy delivered to consumers by electricity, from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035. It sounds wonkish, but could usher in a new age of electricity. A shift to electric vehicles, electric heating and cooling, and modernised heavy industry will cut emissions while slashing global fossil fuel import bills by $720 billion each year. An electrification target may also be easier to land than agreement to phase out fossil fuels. Ironically, given his support for the oil industry, US president Donald Trump has made perhaps the clearest case for electrification. The US war on Iran has triggered the largest disruption of oil supply in history. Demand for clean energy technologies is surging as countries seek alternatives to volatile fossil fuel imports. The exact form of an electrification target at COP31 will be subject to intense negotiations. Australian climate minister Chris Bowen will have his task cut out for him as chief negotiator. In itself, COP31 can’t deliver a silver bullet for climate action. But if it reinforces international cooperation and moves the dial forward on global electrification, hope remains. Wesley Morgan is a fellow at the Climate Council of Australia

(Imperial War Museums)Who do we forget on Remembrance Day? For a long time, histories of the First World War have been popularly understood in a Euro-centric manner. But descendants of Indian soldiers and researchers have long pushed for recognition for the approximately 1.4 million men from current-day India, Pakistan and Bangladesh who helped wage the First World War for the British Empire. Yet when it comes to the war’s impact on British India, many of us still think of contributions as military and masculine. The double portrait of two Sikh risaldars, Jagat Singh and Man Singh, currently on display at the Art Gallery of Ontario is a testament to such recognition. The men hailed from Punjab, the hub of military recruitment known as the “sword arm” of the Raj. The piece was painted in London by Phillip de László two months before the Battle of the Somme in 1916, when many Indian soldiers were wounded or lost their lives. But remembrance is gendered. Historian Radhika Singha has revealed the overlooked role of non-combatants such as labourers, cooks, sweepers and many other essential “follower” roles in the war. Male and militarized remembrance also takes for granted the impact of the war on those women and families the men left behind. As my preliminary research into First World War archives of letters, songs and reports indicate, women bore the consequences of the total war thousands of miles away from the Western Front. Early on, women recognized the gendered cost of the war, and were critical of the reliance on their husbands, sons and fathers to wage it. A recruiting meeting held at one of the hill fairs in India in October 1917. (Press Agency Photographer/India during the First World War, 1914-1918/Imperial War Museums) Compounding gendered hierarchies The impact of the First World War compounded the gendered hierarchies already existing in Punjab. The state of Punjab in northern India was annexed by the East India Company in 1849. Colonial officials were keen to secure political and economic control by joining hands with existing patriarchs and landowners in this agricultural economy. First World War Hindi-language recruitment poster with slogan statement that beings: ‘This soldier defends India. He protects his home and family.’ (Imperial War Museum) But such developments were especially harmful for women. As feminist historian Veena Oldenburg has shown, measures such as the codification of customary law based on consultations with male household heads formalized the dominance of the male landowner. This contributed to making women dependent on the men around them. Colonial officials were also fascinated by the Punjabi peasant because they believed that he embodied war-like qualities. The Darwinian “martial race theory” claimed that only certain men in India could be soldiers. Colonial authorities came to view the Punjabi peasant, who worked the land and had a history of a military tradition, as fighting material. By the turn of the 20th century, these ideas culminated in what researchers termed the “Punjabization of the Indian Army.” On the eve of the First World War, about 60 per cent of the Indian army was made up of Punjabi men. When war broke out, colonial authorities promoted recruitment of local men through further promises of land grants, cash rewards and secure pay, and linked it to the ideas of izzat or honour. How did women respond to the war? While middle class and elite Indian women led campaigns to encourage wives and mothers to send their husbands and sons to war, this response wasn’t universal. Many women in the villages of Punjab tried to prevent their husbands and sons from enlisting. News and letters from the war front revealed the brutal conditions of trench warfare. According to colonial reports of the time, mothers and wives believed that men were not being adequately trained before they were sent off. The colonial government denounced such beliefs as wild rumours. Yet historical evidence shows that women in Punjab tried to hinder recruitment efforts to such an extent that, by December 1914, colonial officials complained that the “tears of womenfolk” had become the biggest hurdle to recruitment. In Amritsar, Punjab, in 1915, an official noted in his diary that women “would trail recruiting parties for several miles, patiently awaiting opportunities to lure away acquired recruits.” Colonial intelligence reports show women would sing songs blaming King George for taking away their husbands and brothers. In these, women offered trenchant critiques of the colonial government, claiming that their men had been used as fodder by the firangi (colonizer). In 2016, Berlin based Pakistani artist Bani Abidi displayed contemporary renditions of folk songs at the Edinburgh Art Festival. Entitled, “Memorial to Lost Words,” this exhibition moves beyond “stone engravings or statues” as sites of memory but combines translated letters and folk songs. Phrases from a translated folk song sing: “Don’t go, don’t go, stay here my friend, the ignorant are packing up and leaving, flowers are withering, friendships are breaking.” Bani Abidi’s Memorial to Lost Words is a sound installation bearing poignant testament to the tragedy of the First World War. Scrambling for survival Women whose husbands enlisted scrambled for money to survive. Delays in the receipt of remittances and pay added to their economic struggles. A collection of letters shows that one wife wrote to her husband in France that she had only received two months’ worth of allowances in six months and had to resort to pawning her jewellery to “keep myself alive.” Conditions had worsened because the entire economy was geared toward the war effort. Famine, plague and influenza added to the troubles. Urdu-language First World War propaganda poster reads: ‘Look at that man. He is doing his duty to his King. He is demonstrating his bravery and making his family proud as well as earning more money than before.’ (Imperial War Museums) But women did not suffer passively. They held their husbands accountable for going to the war. One woman complained to her husband: “I go round begging the neighbours for water and wood, yet you never think of all this.” Some women even used the war to run away with their lovers while their husbands were away, which troubled the men and the colonial government alike. Women’s efforts to hinder recruitment in Punjab, their critique of the colonial government and their letters reveal the complexities of women’s responses to the war. Beyond remembering the male soldier who arrived in Europe, we should also remember those he left behind. Umaima Miraj received funding from the Social Science and Humanities Research Council for this research.
d470c95746552efd: The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management
Originally published on Global Voices
The stunning beauty of the Dominican Republic’s north coast at Los Haitises National Park. Photo by Jason Boldero on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

When you think of the Dominican Republic, the first thing that might come to mind is paradise where sun, sand, and sea combine to offer unforgettable experiences to Dominican families and global travellers alike — but the country’s deep sea is also of critical importance.

Jonathan Delance, director of conservation of the National 30×30 Program of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, says that Dominican marine ecosystems are one of the country’s “greatest natural and strategic riches” — diverse, highly connected, and fundamental to national life.

From an ecological standpoint, coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, dunes, beaches, pelagic zones, and deep-sea ecosystems sustain biodiversity. From an economic and social standpoint, they are the foundation of tourism, fishing, and coastal protection.

Despite relevant research being conducted in the country, information remains limited. According to Delance, some of the available studies on Dominican deep waters have had a geophysical, geochemical, or geological focus, rather than an ecological one. This is largely because deep-sea research is expensive, complex, and requires specialised technology, such as remotely operated vehicles, acoustic equipment, deep-sea cameras, and highly specific taxonomic capabilities.

Precisely because of these limitations, for a long time the National System of Protected Areas lacked a clear representation of deep ecosystems and their underwater geomorphologies, a gap that began to close with the inclusion of the Beata Underwater Ridge as a conservation object within the Orlando Jorge Mera Marine Sanctuary, representing a relevant step forward for the country.

As part of the scientific basis for this process, Delance explains that the technical report on deep-sea fauna documented research between 900 and 4,200 metres deep, recording 1,855 biological observations and 3,294 organisms. One of the most interesting finds was 148 morphospecies, defined in the book Marine Biodiversity as a “group of specimens that can be distinguished from others on the basis of morphological characteristics,” including poriferans, cnidarians, echinoderms, chordates, arthropods, annelids, mollusks, and other yet undetermined organisms.

The pelagic fauna expedition conducted in 2024 covered 2,771 kilometres (1,722 miles) and identified six species of cetaceans, 15 species of birds, as well as sharks and turtle routes. Environmental DNA resulted in the identification of species — including more than 400 morphospecies — along the entire food chain, demonstrating the health and complexity of this space.

Despite these advances, Delance notes, important gaps persist: “We need more information on taxonomic identification at the species level, genetic connectivity, oceanographic dynamics, seasonal distribution, cumulative impacts, biogeography of deep species, and the response of these ecosystems to underwater disturbances, climate change, and other pressures.”
What is deep-sea mining?

According to the International Seabed Authority (ISA), deep-sea mining (DSM) refers to the extraction of mineral resources from deposits located on the deep seabed, typically found between 400 metres (1.300 feet) and 6.5 kilometres (4 miles) beneath the ocean’s surface.

There are three primary types of mineral deposits. Polymetallic nodules (PMN) were discovered on March 7, 1873, during the Challenger expedition; scientists described them as “several peculiar black oval bodies which were composed of almost pure manganese oxide.” The ISA states that they are composed of manganese, iron, silicates, and hydroxides, and can be as small as micro-nodules or as large as 20 centimetres. They are commonly found on the west coast of Mexico in the Pacific Ocean (also known as the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone), as well as the Central Indian Ocean Basin, and the Peru Basin. While polymetallic nodules can be found in lakes, the ones with greater economic value are typically located at depths of 4,000–6,000 metres (2.5 miles–3.7 miles), in areas with an extremely low sedimentation rate.

Polymetallic sulphides (PMS), which contain large amounts of copper, zinc, lead, iron, silver and gold, were first discovered in 1948 as part of the Swedish Albatross oceanographic expedition in the Red Sea. Later, in 1963 and 1966, scientists also found metalliferous muds and brines in the Red Sea Rift System.

Finally, cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (CFC) are found at depths of less than 400 metres (1.300 feet) to more than 5,000 metres (3 miles), mainly in areas with strong volcanic activity. While similar to polymetallic nodules in their composition, these crusts are attracting interest from mining companies because they can contain relatively high amounts of cobalt, as well as platinum, rare earth elements, nickel, and manganese.
The ISA has signed 15-year contracts with 22 contractors for DSM exploration, with most of them covering PMN, eight going to PMS and five to CFC.

The contractors range from national governments — including South Korea, India, Poland and Russia — to research institutes and private companies. A small number, such as South Korea, India and China’s Ocean Mineral Resources Research and Development Association, hold contracts across more than one deposit type, while the majority have a single contract.
The Dominican Republic’s position

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which opened for signature in Montego Bay, Jamaica, in 1982 and entered into force in 1994, establishes the overarching legal framework governing ocean space, marine scientific research and environmental protection.

A central component of the Convention is the definition of “the Area,” the seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. UNCLOS declares the Area and its resources to be the “common heritage of mankind,” and establishes the ISA to administer these resources and regulate their exploration and eventual exploitation.
Between 2020 and 2025, the Dominican Republic had an active participation in the ISA, which is headquartered in Kingston, Jamaica.

At the ISA Assembly (ISBA28) in July 2023, Edward Pérez Reyes, the Dominican Republic’s then representative to the ISA, who twice served as its vice president, presented the country’s position on deep-sea mining. While he recognised the importance of these minerals for an energy transition, the DR advocated for a moratorium until there was a solid legal framework and sufficient scientific evidence to guarantee the protection of marine ecosystems. He also proposed sustainable alternatives, the circular economy, and recycling, as well as an equitable distribution of benefits and strengthening of the management of marine resources.

“The Dominican Republic was never against the International Seabed Authority or the process outlined by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea,” Pérez Reyes, who is now the DR’s ambassador to Japan, explained. “Quite the opposite. We always understood that the international community’s effort to regulate the exploration and eventual exploitation of the seabed was a legitimate exercise. Before that legal framework existed, the risk was that countries with the technological capacity to do so would act on their own. The Convention came precisely to prevent that, and to establish common rules for everyone. So, the discussion was about something else. The question was whether the international community was already in a position to move from exploration to commercial exploitation. Our impression was that it was not yet.”

The DR’s stance, he said — the result of an inter-institutional process involving the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the National Authority for Maritime Affairs (ANAMAR), and more — was never intended to halt the process. Rather, it was to allow science to keep advancing and for the ISA to finish building the regulatory framework that the Convention itself had mandated it to develop. “Every time we learned of a new research study,” Pérez Reyes recalled, “we ended up thinking that there was still much more to know. And that led us back to the same reflection: we had to continue researching before deciding such great consequence.”

Even today, the principles that guided that position still seem valid to him, though the information on which decisions are made can always change. “If science provides new elements, a responsible state has to analyse them,” Pérez Reyes added.

For Delance, scientific exploration of the deep sea is necessary to better understand these ecosystems before considering any form of utilisation. In his view, the DR still lacks key information, including biodiversity baselines, bathymetric and geomorphological maps, data on vulnerable species, ecological connectivity, oceanographic processes, environmental risks, and the resilience of ecosystems.

He believes that the Dominican stance in favour of a precautionary pause in deep-sea mining responds to the need to first generate sufficient scientific evidence to properly plan, regulate, and protect these spaces, and warned that if deep-sea ecosystems are not protected, the DR and wider Caribbean could lose still-unknown biodiversity, genetic resources of potential scientific value, migratory corridors, and essential habitats for threatened species. The country must therefore move, Delance believes, toward marine spatial planning in order to balance conservation and the sustainable use of these strategic ecosystems.
Environmental groups raise opposition

The Magua Ecological Foundation, which is committed to environmental conservation, biodiversity protection, and the sustainable use of natural resources, categorically disapproves of deep-sea mining in the DR, cautioning that the impacts could be severe and irreversible.

Its president, Manuel Alejandro Rodríguez, said that deep-sea mining represents a significant threat to marine ecosystems, whose biological richness and ecological value are fundamental to the well-being of present and future generations. DSM could lead to habitat destruction, species loss, pollution, and disruption of ecological processes, and potentially cause irreversible environmental damage due to the release of metals and other polluting substances into the marine environment.

“In an island nation like the Dominican Republic,” he stressed, “whose seas support extraordinary biodiversity and are essential for activities such as fishing, tourism, scientific research, and the protection of coastal communities, the risks associated with deep-sea mining far outweigh any potential economic benefits.”

Reaffirming the precautionary principle as a fundamental pillar of environmental management, he added, “As long as scientific uncertainties persist regarding the consequences of this activity and there are no guarantees that it can be carried out without causing irreparable damage, it is essential to prioritise the conservation of our marine ecosystems.”

The Foundation wants the authorities, the private sector, scientific community, and society in general to strengthen the protection of our oceans, promote public policies based on the best available scientific evidence, and commit to sustainable development models.

Sixto Inchaustegui, president of Grupo Jaragua, another NGO working for the sustainable management of biodiversity, said that the DR does not know where deep-sea mining activities could take place along its coasts, especially since its continental shelf is very narrow and the country relies heavily on marine and coastal ecosystem services, including tourism, fisheries, and protection against hurricanes. Such ecosystems are already highly threatened and degraded due to land-use changes, mangrove loss, erosion, overfishing, coral mortality, pollution, and other pressures, all of which are being exacerbated by climate change.
New representative to the ISA

On July 14, Ambassador Nancy Patricia Franjul Pérez presented her credentials as the DR’s new permanent representative to the ISA, and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to help develop a solid, transparent, and science-based regulatory framework for the exploitation of mineral resources in the Area.

Franjul Pérez also emphasised the critical role of the ISA at a time when the international community seeks to balance resource security, marine environmental protection, technological development, and the equitable distribution of benefits. ISA Secretary-General Leticia Carvalho said she looks forward to continuing the dialogue, “including on the draft exploitation regulations and the wider work of the Authority, in a spirit of transparency, environmental responsibility, and respect” for the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The future of Dominican marine protection

In 2024, the DR became the first Caribbean country to surpass one of the targets of the global 30×30 environmental commitment, protecting 30.8 percent of its waters. As Delance explained, however, the challenge now is not solely to declare new protected areas, but to ensure they have effective management.

Currently, more than 90 percent of the protected marine area has management plans, a fundamental tool to guide conservation, regulate permitted uses, monitor ecosystems, and support decision-making. Looking to the future, efforts must focus on moving toward effective protection by strengthening monitoring and technological surveillance, regulating maritime traffic, developing national scientific capacity, and generating more research on deep ecosystems.

The DR will participate alongside Colombia in a scientific mission belonging to the inaugural programme of the REV Ocean, the world’s largest ocean research vessel, which will conduct the Beata Ridge mission in 2027.

The expedition will allow for the study of the deep ecosystems of the Beata Underwater Ridge, generate information on its biodiversity and ecological connectivity, and assess potential threats to strengthen ocean conservation and management. The country will also initiate a marine spatial planning process covering both protected and unprotected areas, enabling better organisation of ocean uses and supporting evidence-based decision-making.

6ea945f382f18776: From Ibrahim M Ahmad
The dispute over former prime minister Najib Razak’s proposed transfer from Kajang Prison to house arrest is no longer simply about whether he should go home.

At its core, the controversy raises a broader question: what happens when a royal pardon, a court order and a separate criminal sentence intersect in ways that existing laws do not clearly anticipate?

The latest developments have placed the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC), the prisons department, Najib’s lawyers and even Istana Negara on seemingly different sides of a debate over implementation rather than principle. All parties say they are attempting to uphold the law. The disagreement is over what the law, and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's decree, require in practice.
That distinction is important.

Public discussion has largely centred on whether Najib should be released from prison immediately. Yet the more significant issue may be whether Malaysia’s legal framework adequately addresses a situation in which a prisoner is granted a conditional royal pardon while also facing another custodial sentence.

The King’s position appears straightforward. Najib was granted a conditional pardon allowing him to serve the remainder of his SRC International sentence under house arrest, provided he paid the RM50 million fine imposed by the court. That condition has now been met.
Ordinarily, that would appear to settle the matter.

However, the High Court document issued following payment of the fine has introduced uncertainty over the legal effect of Najib’s "discharge" and whether the SRC sentence continues to run until 2028 or is regarded as completed.

The document, called an “Order of Discharge on Payment of Fine”, directs that Najib be discharged immediately. But it also states that the remainder of his sentence is to be served under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.

The question is what “discharged” means in this context. Does it mean he should leave Kajang Prison and continue serving his SRC sentence at home? Or could it mean that the SRC sentence is legally complete? The AGC says clarification is needed on the effect of the order.
The distinction is far from academic.

Najib’s separate 15-year prison sentence in the 1MDB case was ordered to begin only after the SRC sentence ends. If the SRC sentence continues under house arrest, the chronology is uncomplicated. If it is deemed complete upon payment of the fine, questions arise about whether the 1MDB sentence should begin immediately.
Faced with that uncertainty, the AGC argues that clarification is needed before any transfer takes place.

Critics may see this as an unnecessary delay, particularly after Istana Negara stated that all conditions of the pardon had been fulfilled. Supporters of the AGC’s position, however, contend that resolving ambiguity now is preferable to triggering fresh legal challenges later.
Neither argument is entirely without merit.

What the episode has exposed is a potential gap in Malaysia’s legal architecture. While imprisonment, parole and remission are governed by established laws and procedures, house arrest remains relatively unfamiliar territory. There is no comprehensive statutory framework setting out how such arrangements should operate, how compliance should be monitored or how they interact with other criminal sentences.
That absence has created room for competing interpretations.

The issue also extends beyond Najib himself. Any legal principles established in his case could influence how future pardons are implemented and how exceptional forms of custody are administered. For that reason, the courts’ eventual interpretation may carry implications beyond one high-profile prisoner.
At the same time, there is a public confidence dimension that cannot be ignored.

Najib’s status as a former prime minister means every development is scrutinised through the lens of equality before the law. Many Malaysians will want assurance that whatever outcome emerges is grounded in clear legal principles rather than political considerations or institutional pressure.
That makes transparency critical.
The public deserves a clear explanation of how the pardon is meant to operate, how the prison and court orders interact, and how the separate 1MDB sentence fits into the equation.

Ultimately, the dispute should not become a contest between institutions. The King’s decree, the courts and the executive branch each have defined constitutional roles. The challenge lies in ensuring those roles operate coherently when they overlap.

The immediate question is whether Najib leaves prison or remains there for the time being. The more enduring question is whether Malaysia’s legal system can provide a clear and consistent answer when faced with circumstances that its laws did not expressly anticipate.
That is an issue that extends well beyond Najib Razak.
Ibrahim M Ahmad is an FMT reader.

51322d004c17054c: Dalam dunia politik moden yang penuh dengan kebanjiran maklumat, propaganda tidak lagi beroperasi dengan cara lama yang kasar, memaksa dan terang-terangan. Propaganda hari ini bergerak melalui bahasa, khususnya bahasa yang samar, berlapik, dan mengelirukan.

Menurut Jason Stanley, Profesor Falsafah di Yale University dan penulis buku How Propaganda Works (2015), propaganda moden berjaya bukan kerana ia mengelirukan, tetapi kerana ia menggunakan kebenaran yang difahamkan secara keliru. Bahasa propaganda menjadi alat untuk mengawal fikiran rakyat dengan cara yang lembut, hampir tidak dapat dikesan, namun sangat efektif dalam membentuk apa yang rakyat fikir benar.

Stanley menjelaskan propaganda moden berfungsi dengan cara menghalang wacana kritikal. Ia bukan sekadar menutup akses kepada maklumat, tetapi memanipulasi makna maklumat tersebut sehingga rakyat tidak dapat membuat penilaian rasional.

Bahasa yang digunakan kelihatan profesional, teknikal dan dilihat rasional namun sebenarnya ia menyembunyikan tindakan sebenar atau menutup kegagalan. Contoh mudah: apabila subsidi ditarik balik, ia akan disebut sebagai ‘penstrukturan semula mekanisme bantuan’ atau ‘rasionalisasi subsidi’. Apabila berlaku masalah dalam pentadbiran, kita mendengar frasa ‘isu dalam perhatian’, ‘penilaian sedang dibuat’, atau ‘perkara ini sedang dikaji secara menyeluruh’. Semua ayat ini nampak sopan dan meyakinkan, tetapi jika diteliti secara mendalam, ia tidak menjelaskan apa-apa pun.

Seni propaganda melalui bahasa samar ini berfungsi kerana ia memenuhi dua keperluan politik: pertama, menjaga imej pemerintah; kedua, menenangkan rakyat supaya tidak panik. Stanley membahagikan propaganda kepada dua kategori.
Supporting propaganda menggunakan bahasa yang kelihatan menyokong nilai demokrasi seperti ketelusan, profesionalisme dan kestabilan, tetapi tujuan sebenarnya ialah mengekalkan kuasa pemerintah.

Undermining propaganda pula ialah bahasa yang kelihatan rasional tetapi digunakan untuk menutup ketidakjujuran atau tindakan yang bertentangan dengan kepentingan awam. Kedua-duanya menggunakan bahasa yang sama iaitu kabur, berlapik, dan sabar berfungsi dalam konteks yang berbeza.

Dalam masyarakat moden, bahasa berlapik digunakan untuk mengurus persepsi dan emosi rakyat. Apabila isu sensitif timbul seperti kenaikan harga barang, kegagalan projek mega, kelemahan institusi, atau ketegangan kaum, pemerintah cenderung memilih frasa-frasa yang menenangkan. ‘Mengawal tekanan ekonomi global’, ‘menyelaraskan semula struktur fiskal’, ‘memperkukuh ekosistem pentadbiran’, atau ‘melakukan penambahbaikan proses’. Semuanya adalah contoh bagaimana bahasa digunakan untuk melunakkan realiti. Rakyat mendengar perkataan yang sedap, tetapi tidak memahami apakah tindakan sebenar yang sedang dilakukan.

Stanley menegaskan propaganda moden juga bekerja melalui kebanjiran maklumat. Dalam sistem di mana media dikawal secara langsung atau tidak langsung, maklumat satu sisi menjadi norma. Rakyat bergantung kepada ‘kebenaran rasmi’, dan bahasa pemerintah menjadi bahasa media.

Maka. gaya bahasa berlapik yang sama diulang melalui berita, kenyataan akhbar, laporan ekonomi dan ucapan pemimpin. Ulangan ini akhirnya menjadikan bahasa propaganda sebagai bahasa biasa. Rakyat tidak menyedari mereka sedang dipengaruhi, kerana bahasa yang digunakan bukan bahasa kasar atau menipu, tetapi bahasa yang nampak profesional.

Bahasa samar juga digunakan untuk mencipta musuh yang tidak bernama. Teknik ini sangat berkesan kerana ia menanam emosi tanpa perlu membuktikan apa-apa. Ungkapan seperti ‘pihak tertentu sedang cuba menggugat kestabilan negara’, ‘agenda asing sedang menyusup’, atau ‘unsur ekstrem tidak boleh dipandang ringan’ sering digunakan tanpa identiti jelas.

Rakyat mendengar ancaman, merasai kebimbangan, tetapi tidak mengetahui siapa musuh sebenar. Inilah teknik propaganda yang menanam rasa takut secara terkawal dan sekali gus memberikan justifikasi kepada tindakan pemerintah untuk bertindak keras, menggubal undang-undang tambahan atau mengawal ruang awam.

Dalam konteks Malaysia, budaya bahasa berlapik sudah lama berakar. Ketika isu perkauman timbul, istilah ‘sensitiviti masyarakat’ digunakan untuk mengelakkan perbincangan terus tentang diskriminasi atau ketidaksamarataan.

Ketika berlaku skandal, istilah ‘ketirisan kecil’ digunakan. Ketika ekonomi merosot, istilah ‘penyesuaian struktur ekonomi’ menjadi pilihan. Apabila kerajaan gagal mengurus bencana, ungkapan ‘cabaran penyelarasan’ digunakan bagi mengalihkan perhatian daripada kelemahan pengurusan. Bahasa ini tidak salah, tetapi ia menjarakkan rakyat daripada memahami realiti sebenar.

Propaganda melalui bahasa samar bekerja bukan dengan cara memaksa rakyat percaya sesuatu, tetapi dengan cara mengisi ruang antara penjelasan dan kekeliruan. Rakyat yang tidak mendapat maklumat sebenar akhirnya membina naratif sendiri berdasarkan andaian dan perasaan.

Inilah yang dimaksudkan Stanley apabila beliau mengatakan propaganda moden adakalanya memanipulasi rasional manusia. Ia mengehadkan rakyat untuk berfikir, tetapi mendidik mereka menerima kabus sebagai kebenaran.

Dalam era digital, bahasa samar menjadi lebih penting kerana maklumat tersebar dengan pantas. Propagandis perlu mengurus persepsi dengan cepat, dan bahasa berlapik memberikan mereka masa. Satu kenyataan kabur sudah cukup untuk menghentikan kritikan selama 24 jam, sementara strategi komunikasi seterusnya disusun. Contohnya, ketika berlaku masalah dalam sesuatu operasi kenyataan seperti ‘sistem sedang dipertingkatkan’ atau ‘masalah teknikal sedang diselesaikan’ membantu menutup tekanan awam sementara ruang masa dicari boleh menyelesaikan masalah.

Kesannya, rakyat berdepan dunia yang penuh dengan ayat tetapi kosong makna. Mereka mendengar banyak perkataan, tetapi sedikit fakta. Mereka rasa diberi maklumat, tetapi sebenarnya menerima secara samar. Propaganda paling berjaya ialah propaganda yang menjadikan rakyat percaya mereka memahami sesuatu isu padahal mereka tidak diberi maklumat sebenar.

Jason Stanley merumuskan hal ini dengan tepat iaitu: ‘Propaganda ialah manipulasi kehendak rasional manusia sehingga perbincangan terhenti’. Inilah kekuatan gaya bahasa samar dan berlapik. Ia bukan hanya menutup kebenaran, tetapi menutup pintu untuk bertanya.
Dan selama pintu itu tertutup, propaganda menguasai seluruh ruang pemikiran masyarakat.

c6e7cabff185da96: An extract from Plato's "Republic" reads: "Said the old Cephalus to the younger Socrates, 'Older men of my age flock together and in our meeting my common tale is – I cannot eat, I cannot drink, the pleasure of youth and love have fled away, there was a good time once, but now gone, and life is no longer ours.'"
Such is the reality of ageing, and perhaps there is a lesson here for politicians who have overstayed their welcome in the political arena.
I hope that the impending Melaka state election will be an eye-opener for Malaysians, particularly our political leaders who seem to have difficulty recognising when it is time to call it a day.
PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang and many politicians of his generation should seriously consider retiring from politics.
Judging from their regular outbursts and political pronouncements, some appear increasingly disconnected from the realities, aspirations and concerns of ordinary Malaysians.
Their political vocabulary, arguments and preoccupations seem to belong to another era.
Hadi's latest outburst is a case in point.
In his reaction to the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) between opposition MPs and the government, he likened the arrangement to the deception of the Dajjal.

Whatever one's views about the CSA, surely there are more constructive ways to debate a parliamentary arrangement. It is one thing to disagree with a political agreement; it is quite another to invoke apocalyptic religious imagery to discredit it.
Such rhetoric does little to advance public understanding or the quality of our political discourse.
Malaysia is rapidly changing
This is precisely the problem with some of our ageing political leaders. They seem more interested in fighting yesterday's political battles than addressing tomorrow's challenges.
Our younger population is concerned about employment, housing affordability, wages, education, technology, artificial intelligence, green agenda and the rising cost of living.
They want practical solutions, economic opportunities and a government that understands the world they are growing up in.
Yet much of our political conversation remains trapped in old rivalries, identity politics, religious arguments and endless disputes over who should be in power and who should become prime minister.
How much longer must Malaysians listen to identity and religious politics from the same personalities with the same political arguments?

Hadi is not alone. Former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, former federal minister Rais Yatim and several other long-serving political figures should seriously consider leaving the political arena as well.

They have had their opportunities, occupied important positions and exercised considerable influence over the country's political upheavals. They should recognise that political leadership is not a lifetime entitlement.

There is a difference between serving the country and holding on to political power. After decades in politics, surely there comes a time when personal ambition must give way to institutional renewal.

Our political parties should not be personal properties, nor should their leadership positions become permanent appointments. No individual should be indispensable to a political party, let alone to an entire nation.
Malaysia's political weakness

One of Malaysia's biggest political weaknesses is the reluctance of senior politicians to groom and give way to younger leaders. They continue to dominate party structures, determine candidate selections and control political narratives.
Young politicians are often expected to wait patiently for their turn, while the same senior personalities continue to occupy the top positions election after election.
This is unhealthy.
A political party cannot produce new leaders or renew its leadership in a hierarchy that is dominated by ageing politicians. PAS, Bersatu and Umno are clear examples.
Do they genuinely believe in the future of their parties or are they simply protecting their own positions?
I fully agree with the argument about giving younger politicians greater opportunities.

The emergence of younger leaders should not merely be an electoral gimmick to attract younger voters. They must be given real responsibilities, decision-making authority and opportunities to shape national policies.
Of course, being young does not automatically make someone a capable leader. Experience, integrity, competence and sound judgment matter.

But these qualities cannot be the exclusive possessions of older politicians, either. Young leaders need opportunities to acquire experience, and they cannot do so if the older generation refuses to release its grip.

Let the younger generation make mistakes, learn from them and develop their own leadership capabilities. That is how political maturity is built. We cannot keep telling young people that they lack experience while denying them the opportunity to gain it.

There is also a larger democratic question. How can we expect a country to embrace new ideas, modernise its institutions and prepare for the future when much of its political leadership remains occupied by personalities whose political careers began several decades ago?
The world is moving on
Technology, economic structures, international competition and the expectations of younger citizens are changing. Political leadership must change with them.
For Hadi, Muhyiddin, Zahid and scores of others who have spent much of their lives in politics, perhaps the greatest contribution they can now make is to step aside gracefully.

They can offer advice, share their experience and allow the next generation to take responsibility. They do not need to remain party presidents, political kingmakers or permanent fixtures in our national politics.

The Melaka election should be more than another contest between political coalitions. It should also be an opportunity for voters to consider the kind of leadership they want for the next decade and beyond.

Malaysia needs a political generation that looks forward, not backwards; one that debates policies rather than personalities, solves problems rather than manufactures controversies, and builds institutions rather than protects individual political careers.
Enough is enough. You have had your time. You have had your opportunities. It is time to let go.

3b237e183dd5187e: Malaysians have come to take our festivals for granted, gliding through Deepavali as if it were just another ordinary day on the calendar—a polite pause amid the roar of traffic and the clatter of daily life.

Yet, if we close our eyes for a moment and picture it—houses alive with oil lamps glowing in every direction, the air fragrant with sesame-scented murukku, and the laughter of children in new clothes spilling onto the streets—we are reminded of the festival's vibrant soul.
What few of us realise, however, is that this radiant celebration once rose in daring rebellion.
Today, Deepavali burns brightly as a public holiday across Peninsular Malaysia, with Sabah having quietly folded it into its own calendar of observances.

But few know the breathless, dramatic saga of how this festival was once locked in a fierce, cinematic battle for supremacy—not merely over lamps and sweets, but for the very right to be recognised as a national holiday.
That epic contest was fought not against external forces, but between two towering pillars of the Hindu community itself: Deepavali and Thaipusam.

Both claimed the same prize: a full public holiday so their celebrations could soar to their unbridled heights. One side believed Deepavali, with its blaze of lights that welcomed every soul under the sun, was the broader, more inclusive flame that would carry Indian identity into the future. The other saw in Thaipusam—with its profound message of inner victory through devotion and discipline—the sacred, undying fire that needed to be nurtured.
The battle was real, heated, and decided in colonial Singapore in 1914—a moment that still echoes today, though almost all of us remain blissfully unaware of it.
I wonder how many Malaysians—Indians among them—know that the first Indian-related public holiday in British Malaya was actually for Thaipusam?

Then spelled Tai-pusum, it first flickered into existence in the 1879 Holidays Ordinance IX as a bank holiday in Penang. In British Malaya, bank holidays existed primarily to ensure the colony's commercial engine paused simultaneously.

Thaipusam secured its spot because of a dynamic Indian merchant class in Penang and because government departments, most notably the Public Works Department and the municipal council, were overwhelmingly staffed by Indians.

Then came 1914. The colonial administration decided that one set of uniform public holidays should cover the entire Straits Settlements. Operating under the rule of "one major festival of each of the main races," a Bill was drafted nominating Thaipusam for the Indian community as it was already a holiday in Penang.

Here the story takes a twist. The English-speaking elites and merchants of Singapore preferred Deepavali. Their community was a diverse tapestry woven from Telugus, Gujaratis, Sindhis, Malayalees, and Punjabis—not just Tamils. Thaipusam, they argued, was too narrow, too tied to the Chettiar community, and too purely religious for their cosmopolitan vision.
Led by the formidable Dr N Veerasamy Naidu—one of Singapore’s first Indian doctors and a municipal commissioner—the merchant group petitioned Governor Sir Arthur Henderson Young.

Their letter glowed with eloquence and loyalty, speaking of making Deepavali “an act of grace which will be greatly appreciated not only by the 60 or 70,000 most loyal and submissive subjects of His most gracious Majesty the Emperor of India but by the future generations of the permanent residents of the colony”.
They reminded the governor that Deepavali was already observed as a public holiday in India and that it was a public holiday in Singapore in the year 1912.

The movement quickly gained momentum. In February 1914, roughly a thousand prominent Hindus packed the Hindu Association on Belilios Road. Veerasamy, who chaired the meeting, reminded those present that Deepavali had been declared a holiday in Singapore in 1912, thanks to an earlier petition through the Hindu and Muhammadan Endowments Board. Yet a similar application in 1913 had not succeeded.
Now the stakes were higher — the holiday would cover the whole colony. And it would not require annual petitions.

Among those present were influential merchants and elites such as MV Pillay, SMR Naidu, KN Kothary, Nagar Das, Chotiirmal, M Soomapah, Mungul Singh, Dr Bardhan, Veer Singh, Thambyrajah, Veeraragava Aiyar, Singaram Pillai and Sivakadacha Padayachi.

Leaders like MV Pillay argued passionately that Deepavali suited Singapore’s multi-racial fabric better, allowing other races to share in its social joy, whereas Thaipusam remained a strictly intense, specialised Hindu observance.

Noting that Deepavali was a public holiday in India, Pillay insisted the same should apply in the Straits Settlements of Singapore, Penang and Malacca (now Melaka). He added that Indian workers in the PWD and municipal council in Singapore were usually given a holiday on Deepavali day and not Thaipusam day.

The meeting adopted a proposal to send a delegation to convince Governor Young to make Deepavali the public holiday for Hindus in the colony. MV Pillay, who moved the motion, claimed that it was the Chettiar community that was pushing for Thaipusam, and that in doing so it had disregarded the wishes of other communities.

Not everyone agreed with this resolution. Some Singapore Hindus, including those not from the Chettiar community, wrote directly to the governor insisting the original Bill remain unchanged. They claimed that Veerasamy’s group did not speak for everyone and that the government would earn the deep gratitude of the community by following Penang's example.

A fierce but polite battle ensued between supporters of both festivals. Ultimately, the British authorities chose to listen to the Singapore merchant class and the more influential English-speaking elites.
They dropped Thaipusam from the Bill and substituted it with Deepavali, passing the Holidays (Amendment) Ordinance 1914 for the entire colony of Singapore, Penang, and Malacca.

I was unable to find any record that showed strong protests from Penang and Malacca Hindus. I suspect the Chettiars - a small, self-reliant and self-effacing mercantile community that prefers to conduct its business in quiet dignity - decided that Thaipusam would still be observed with due respect even if it was no longer an official holiday.

But the ripple effect soon reached the Federated Malay States (FMS). By April 1915, KT Parmanan Pillay, president of the Sri Mahamariamman Temple on High Street (Jalan Tun HS Lee), wrote to Selangor Resident Edward George Broadrick, telling him that the local Hindu community had passed a resolution asking for both Thaipusam and Deepavali to be declared public holidays.

In Taiping, then the capital of Perak, a public meeting was held in the town hall on Feb 21, 1926 under the chairmanship of H Rethinasamy Pillai, reportedly attended by Indians from several parts of the FMS. The meeting resolved to urge the British authorities to also make Deepavali a public holiday in the FMS, as there was then none for the community.

One of the leaders, V Murugasu Pillai, in a letter to the chief secretary to the FMS government Sir William George Maxwell, noted that Deepavali was already a holiday in the neighbouring Straits Settlements. He claimed that the views of the “Indian and Ceylonese communities” in Selangor, Negri Sembilan and Pahang had also been obtained and that all of them were unanimous in voicing the request for a holiday for Deepavali.

Whether the colonial authorities fully capitulated back then remains slightly murky in the archives, but the framework of history eventually birthed the national holiday we enjoy today under the 1951 Holidays Act.
Today, Deepavali’s lights burn brightly across Malaysia, while in several states, Thaipusam remains a powerful public holiday observed with equal vitality.

Ultimately, the story of Deepavali’s rise is one of quiet endurance rather than conquest. Two great flames once stood at opposite ends of the Hindu night sky—one broad and welcoming, the other focused and sacred. Colonial hands chose one over the other a century ago, but time has proven that neither had to be extinguished.

Today, both Deepavali and Thaipusam light up the Malaysian landscape side by side, proving that traditions fought for with such passion never truly fade. They simply learn to glow together, year after year, across the same land.
Happy Deepavali.
